nodes.name: Variables & Assignment
nodes.description: Variables are named references that store values in memory using the assignment operator (=).
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner can correctly assign, update, and read values stored in variables without confusing assignment with equality.
nodes.micro_lesson:
A variable is like a labeled container. Use `=` to assign a value:
```python
x = 10
x = x + 5  # x is now 15
```
The right side evaluates first, then binds to the name on the left.
teach_back_rubric: Mentions that = assigns values from right to left
Explains that variables store or reference values in memory
Distinguishes assignment from mathematical equality

sample_problem.title: Variable Assignment & Update
sample_problem.prompt: Assign variable `score = 50`, then add 25 to it so `score` becomes 75. Return `score`.
sample_problem.starter_code:
def get_updated_score():
    score = 50
    # your code here
    return score

nodes.name: Data Types
nodes.description: Python data types classify data into integers (int), floating points (float), text (str), and truth values (bool).
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner chooses appropriate types and understands type incompatibilities (e.g. adding string to int).
nodes.micro_lesson:
Data has a type that governs what operations are valid:
```python
age = 20          # int
price = 19.99     # float
name = 'Alice'    # str
is_active = True  # bool
```
Mixing incompatible types (e.g. `'5' + 5`) raises a `TypeError`.
teach_back_rubric: Names common primitive types: int, float, str, bool
Explains that data types determine valid operations
Mentions type errors occur when incompatible types are combined

sample_problem.title: String to Integer Conversion
sample_problem.prompt: Convert string `num_str = '42'` into an integer and add 8. Return the sum.

nodes.name: Arithmetic Operators
nodes.description: Operators perform mathematical calculations on numbers (+, -, *, /, //, %, **).
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner can correctly apply division types (/ vs //) and remainder operations (%).
nodes.micro_lesson:
Python provides standard arithmetic:
```python
7 / 2   # 3.5  (float division)
7 // 2  # 3    (integer / floor division)
7 % 2   # 1    (modulo / remainder)
2 ** 3  # 8    (exponentiation)
```
teach_back_rubric: Explains difference between float division (/) and floor division (//)
Explains modulo (%) as returning the remainder of division
Identifies standard operator precedence

sample_problem.title: Calculate Remainder
sample_problem.prompt: Return the remainder when `dividend` is divided by `divisor`.
sample_problem.starter_code:
def remainder(dividend, divisor):
    return dividend % divisor

nodes.name: Comparison Operators
nodes.description: Operators that evaluate relational conditions between expressions and produce a boolean result (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=).
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner uses == for equality testing rather than assignment =, and interprets compound inequalities correctly.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Comparison operators always return `True` or `False`:
```python
x = 5
x == 5   # True (equality check)
x != 3   # True (inequality check)
x <= 4   # False
```
Critical rule: `=` assigns a value; `==` compares two values.
teach_back_rubric: Explicitly contrasts == (comparison) with = (assignment)
Explains that comparison expressions evaluate to boolean True or False
Lists at least 3 comparison operators (<, >, ==, !=, <=, >=)

sample_problem.title: Check Equality
sample_problem.prompt: Write a function `is_positive(n)` returning `True` if `n > 0`, otherwise `False`.
sample_problem.starter_code:
def is_positive(n):
    return n > 0
sample_problem.test_harness:
assert is_positive(5) is True
assert is_positive(-2) is False
assert is_positive(0) is False
print('Pass!')

nodes.name: Boolean Logic
nodes.description: Logical operators (and, or, not) combine or invert boolean expressions.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner correctly applies truth tables for and/or and understands short-circuit evaluation.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Combine conditions with `and`, `or`, and `not`:
```python
(x > 0) and (x < 10)  # True only if BOTH sides are True
(x == 0) or (x == 1)  # True if AT LEAST ONE side is True
not is_valid          # Inverts True to False and vice versa
```
teach_back_rubric: Explains that 'and' requires both operands to be True
Explains that 'or' requires at least one operand to be True
Explains that 'not' inverts the truth value

sample_problem.title: Range Check with Logical And
sample_problem.prompt: Write a function `in_bounds(val, low, high)` returning `True` if `val >= low` and `val <= high`.
sample_problem.starter_code:
def in_bounds(val, low, high):
    return val >= low and val <= high
sample_problem.test_harness:
assert in_bounds(5, 1, 10) is True
assert in_bounds(0, 1, 10) is False
assert in_bounds(10, 1, 10) is True
print('Pass!')

nodes.name: Conditionals (if/elif/else)
nodes.description: Branching statements (if, elif, else) that execute different blocks of code based on whether a condition evaluates to True.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner constructs mutually exclusive branches and understands that only the first matching branch executes.
teach_back_rubric: Explains that code inside an 'if' block executes only when the condition is True
Explains that elif allows testing additional mutually exclusive conditions
Explains that else acts as a catch-all when all preceding conditions evaluate to False
Mentions that only the first satisfied branch executes

sample_problem.title: Branch on Number Sign
sample_problem.prompt: Write `number_sign(n)` returning `'positive'` if n > 0, `'negative'` if n < 0, and `'zero'` if n == 0.
sample_problem.test_harness:
assert number_sign(10) == 'positive'
assert number_sign(-5) == 'negative'
assert number_sign(0) == 'zero'
print('Pass!')

nodes.name: While Loops
nodes.description: Repetition structure that continues executing a block of code as long as a boolean condition remains True.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner includes state modification within the loop body to ensure loop termination and avoid infinite loops.
nodes.micro_lesson:
A `while` loop repeats while its condition stays True:
```python
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1  # MUST update counter, or loop never ends!
```
If the condition never becomes False, the program hangs in an infinite loop.
teach_back_rubric: Explains that while loops repeat as long as condition is True
Identifies the cause of infinite loops (condition never becoming False)
Mentions loop variable must be modified within loop body

sample_problem.title: Countdown Sum
sample_problem.prompt: Use a while loop to sum numbers from `n` down to 1. Return the total.
sample_problem.test_harness:
assert countdown_sum(5) == 15
assert countdown_sum(1) == 1
assert countdown_sum(0) == 0
print('Pass!')

nodes.name: For Loops & Ranges
nodes.description: Iteration structure that iterates over elements of a sequence (or generated range of numbers) one by one.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner configures range(start, stop, step) bounds correctly, recognizing that stop is non-inclusive.
nodes.micro_lesson:
`for` loops iterate through sequences cleanly:
```python
for i in range(1, 4):  # generates 1, 2, 3 (4 is excluded!)
    print(i)
```
The target variable (`i`) automatically takes each next value on each iteration.
teach_back_rubric: Explains that for loops iterate through elements of a sequence or range
Notes that the stop parameter in range() is non-inclusive
Contrasts for loops (finite sequence) with while loops (condition-based)

sample_problem.title: Sum with For Loop
sample_problem.prompt: Write `sum_evens(limit)` returning the sum of all even numbers from 2 up to `limit` (inclusive).
sample_problem.test_harness:
assert sum_evens(6) == 12  # 2 + 4 + 6
assert sum_evens(10) == 30
assert sum_evens(1) == 0
print('Pass!')

nodes.name: Lists & Collections
nodes.description: Mutable ordered sequences of elements enclosed in square brackets [item1, item2].
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner creates lists, appends items, and iterates over list elements.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Lists hold ordered elements:
```python
items = [10, 20, 30]
items.append(40)     # adds to end: [10, 20, 30, 40]
len(items)           # 4
```
Lists are mutable, meaning their contents can be altered in place.
teach_back_rubric: Explains that lists are ordered collections of items
Mentions that lists are mutable (can add/remove elements)
Demonstrates basic append or access syntax

sample_problem.title: Collect Positive Numbers
sample_problem.prompt: Return a new list containing only the positive numbers (> 0) from `numbers`.

nodes.name: Indexing & Slicing
nodes.description: Accessing individual sequence elements by 0-based offset `seq[i]` or extracting sub-sequences `seq[start:stop]`.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner handles 0-indexing without off-by-one errors and understands negative indices.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Indices count from 0:
```python
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]
nums[0]   # 10 (first)
nums[-1]  # 40 (last)
nums[1:3] # [20, 30] (start index 1 up to but NOT including 3)
```
teach_back_rubric: Explains that indexing starts at 0, not 1
Explains that negative index -1 accesses the final item
Explains that slice stop boundaries are exclusive

sample_problem.title: Extract First and Last
sample_problem.prompt: Return a list `[first, last]` from a non-empty list `items`.
sample_problem.starter_code:
def first_and_last(items):
    return [items[0], items[-1]]

nodes.name: Variable Scope
nodes.description: The visibility and lifetime of variables depending on where they are defined (local to a function vs global).
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner understands that variables assigned inside a function are local and vanish when the function returns.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Scope defines where a variable can be seen:
```python
x = 100  # Global scope

def test():
    y = 50   # Local to test()
    return y

# Accessing y here raises NameError: name 'y' is not defined!
```
Each function call has its own isolated namespace.
teach_back_rubric: Explains difference between local and global variables
Mentions that local variables cannot be accessed outside their defining function
Identifies that every function call creates its own local scope

sample_problem.title: Local Scope Isolation
sample_problem.prompt: Demonstrate local calculation inside `compute(a)` returning `a * 2` without modifying any global state.

nodes.name: Functions & Abstraction
nodes.description: Reusable, named blocks of code defined with `def` that encapsulate logic and can be called from multiple places.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner distinguishes defining a function from invoking it, and organizes code into callable blocks.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Functions package reusable actions:
```python
def greet(name):
    return f'Hello, {name}!'

# Defining does not execute it! You must invoke it:
msg = greet('Ada')  # msg receives 'Hello, Ada!'
```
teach_back_rubric: Distinguishes between function definition (def) and function invocation/calling
Explains how functions promote code reuse and modularity
Describes how arguments are passed into parameters

sample_problem.title: Define Square Function
sample_problem.prompt: Write a function `square(x)` that returns the square of `x`.
sample_problem.starter_code:
def square(x):
    return x * x
sample_problem.test_harness:
assert square(4) == 16
assert square(-3) == 9
assert square(0) == 0
print('Pass!')

nodes.name: Parameters & Arguments
nodes.description: Parameters are variables defined in a function signature; arguments are concrete values supplied during invocation.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner maps positional arguments to parameter names and handles multiple inputs accurately.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Parameters act as placeholders inside the function:
```python
def multiply(a, b):  # a and b are parameters
    return a * b

multiply(4, 7)       # 4 and 7 are arguments
```
Arguments are bound to parameters positionally by default.
teach_back_rubric: Distinguishes parameters (signature placeholders) from arguments (actual runtime values)
Explains how values are passed positionally into function parameters
Mentions what happens when wrong number of arguments is provided

sample_problem.title: Rectangle Area Function
sample_problem.prompt: Write `rect_area(width, height)` accepting two numeric parameters and returning their product.
sample_problem.starter_code:
def rect_area(width, height):
    return width * height

nodes.name: Return Values & Output
nodes.description: The `return` keyword terminates a function and sends a computed result back to the caller (contrasted with print).
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner differentiates return (sending a value to the caller) from print (writing to console) and captures return values.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Printing displays text; returning sends data back:
```python
def bad_add(a, b):
    print(a + b)      # Only shows on screen! Returns None!

def good_add(a, b):
    return a + b     # Sends the value back so caller can use it!

x = good_add(2, 3)    # x is now 5
```
`return` immediately exits the function frame.
teach_back_rubric: Explicitly contrasts returning a value with printing to the console
Explains that return terminates the function immediately
Explains that the caller receives and can store or use the returned value

sample_problem.title: Return Value Calculation
sample_problem.prompt: Write `double(x)` that returns `x * 2` (do not just print it).
sample_problem.starter_code:
def double(x):
    return x * 2
sample_problem.test_harness:
res = double(7)
assert res == 14, f'Expected 14, got {res}'
assert res is not None, 'Function must return a value, not None'
print('Pass!')

nodes.name: Call Stack & Execution Frames
nodes.description: The LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) runtime memory structure that tracks active function calls, their local frames, and return addresses.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner visualizes that calling a function pushes a stack frame and returning pops it, with parent execution suspended in the meantime.
nodes.micro_lesson:
When function `A` calls function `B`:
1. A's execution pauses; its variables stay frozen in its stack frame.
2. B's frame is pushed to the top of the Call Stack.
3. When B returns, its frame is popped, and A resumes right where it left off with B's return value.
Every active call occupies a frame on the stack.
teach_back_rubric: Explains that the call stack is a LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) memory structure
Explains that each function call pushes a new frame storing local variables
Explains that returning pops the frame and resumes the caller
Mentions that parent calls pause while child calls execute

sample_problem.title: Nested Call Stack Execution
sample_problem.prompt: Write `outer(n)` that calls `inner(n)` which returns `n + 10`, and `outer` doubles that result.

nodes.name: Base Case Termination
nodes.description: The non-recursive conditional branch in a recursive function that returns a direct answer and stops further recursion.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner correctly identifies the minimal input condition (e.g. n <= 1) and returns a fixed value without calling the function again.
nodes.micro_lesson:
The base case is the emergency brake of recursion:
```python
def countdown(n):
    if n <= 0:         # <-- BASE CASE!
        return 'Blastoff!'
    return countdown(n - 1)
```
Without a base case (or if the base case condition is never met), the function calls itself indefinitely until Python throws `RecursionError`.
teach_back_rubric: Identifies the base case as the condition that stops recursion
Explains that the base case returns a concrete value without calling the function again
Explains that omitting the base case leads to infinite recursion / RecursionError
Connects base case directly to conditional statements (if condition)

sample_problem.title: Implement Base Case
sample_problem.prompt: Write `sum_to_one(n)`. When `n <= 1`, it should hit the base case and return `1`. Otherwise, return `n + sum_to_one(n - 1)`.

nodes.name: Recursive Step & Subproblems
nodes.description: The branch where a function calls itself with a strictly smaller or simpler input, progressing toward the base case.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner modifies the input argument in the self-call (e.g. n - 1 or lst[1:]) so state moves toward the base case.
nodes.micro_lesson:
The recursive step solves a slice of the problem and delegates the rest:
```python
# In factorial(n):
return n * factorial(n - 1)  # (n - 1) moves closer to 1!
```
The recursive call MUST move toward the base case. If you pass `n` instead of `n - 1`, the problem never shrinks!
teach_back_rubric: Explains that the recursive step calls the same function with a smaller subproblem
Explains that each step must progress toward the base case
Mentions how results from subproblems are combined to form the final result

sample_problem.title: Recursive Progression
sample_problem.prompt: Write `count_steps(n)` that returns 0 if n <= 0, otherwise returns `1 + count_steps(n - 1)`.

nodes.name: Recursion (General)
nodes.description: A problem-solving technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller instances until reaching a base case.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner combines a valid base case conditional check with a progressing recursive call, understanding how the call stack unwinds.
teach_back_rubric: Must identify the base case and explain what stops the recursion
Must explain the recursive step and how arguments shrink toward the base case
Must describe how the call stack unwinds to combine returned values

sample_problem.title: Recursive Factorial
sample_problem.prompt: Implement `factorial(n)` recursively. Return 1 if n <= 1; otherwise return n * factorial(n - 1).
sample_problem.test_harness:
assert factorial(1) == 1, 'factorial(1) must be 1'
assert factorial(0) == 1, 'factorial(0) must be 1'
assert factorial(5) == 120, 'factorial(5) must be 120'
assert factorial(3) == 6, 'factorial(3) must be 6'
print('All factorial tests passed!')

nodes.name: Tree Recursion
nodes.description: A recursive pattern where a function makes two or more recursive calls within a single execution frame, forming a call tree.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner recognizes branching recursion patterns (e.g. Fibonacci) and understands the exponential growth of frames.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Tree recursion calls itself multiple times per frame:
```python
def fib(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)  # Two branching calls!
```
Execution branches into a tree structure before unwinding.
teach_back_rubric: Explains that tree recursion involves multiple recursive calls per frame
Visualizes execution as a branching tree of calls
Contrasts single linear recursion with branching tree recursion

sample_problem.title: Recursive Fibonacci
sample_problem.prompt: Write `fib(n)` returning the nth Fibonacci number (fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2)).
sample_problem.test_harness:
assert fib(0) == 0
assert fib(1) == 1
assert fib(6) == 8
print('Pass!')

nodes.name: Accumulator Pattern in Recursion
nodes.description: Carrying running results forward through an extra function parameter rather than accumulating on the stack unwinding phase.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner passes updated state in parameter arguments (tail recursion style) to accumulate results on the way down.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Instead of waiting for the stack to unwind, accumulate as you go:
```python
def sum_acc(n, acc=0):
    if n <= 0:
        return acc
    return sum_acc(n - 1, acc + n)  # acc accumulates on the way down
```
teach_back_rubric: Explains that an accumulator parameter carries running state forward
Contrasts accumulating on the way down vs on the way up during unwinding
Identifies base case returns the final accumulator value

sample_problem.title: Factorial with Accumulator
sample_problem.prompt: Write `fact_acc(n, acc=1)` accumulating the product forward.

nodes.name: Recursive Call Stack Tracing
nodes.description: The analytical process of tracing nested recursive activation records and verifying parameter values at each unwinding stage.
nodes.mastery_signal: Learner can step through a recursive call stack frame-by-frame on paper or mentally to predict return values.
nodes.micro_lesson:
Tracing recursion is like walking down and up stairs:
1. Going Down: push frames `f(3) -> f(2) -> f(1)`.
2. Hitting Floor: `f(1)` returns base value `1`.
3. Climbing Up: `f(2)` computes `2 * 1 = 2`, `f(3)` computes `3 * 2 = 6`.
teach_back_rubric: Describes both the winding (call) and unwinding (return) phases
Explains how each frame keeps its own private copy of parameters
Tracks the progression of return values back to the initial caller

sample_problem.title: Max Depth Trace
sample_problem.prompt: Write `depth_trace(n)` returning the depth reached when n reaches 0.
